questions.title: Tell me about yourself, tailored to the AI COE Engineering Lead role
questions.quick: I am Rajasekhar Pigilam, a technical architect and full-stack engineering lead with more than 17 years in software engineering, solution architecture and technical leadership. I have built enterprise SaaS, CRM, ERP, EdTech and healthcare platforms using Angular, React, Node.js, NestJS, PostgreSQL and AWS, and I lead through architecture reviews, standards and mentoring. I use Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Claude and ChatGPT daily, and I work with LLM integrations, RAG and agentic ideas. This role joins delivery leadership with AI, and I am building my Power Platform depth for it.
questions.revision: Present role, depth in enterprise platforms, AI-assisted practice, honest Power Platform gap with a plan, and why the AI COE role is the next step.
questions.detailed:
This is the **90-second answer** for the WPP AI COE Engineering Lead interview. Speak it, do not read it.

## Spoken script (about 90 seconds)

"I am Rajasekhar Pigilam, a technical architect and fullstack engineering lead with more than 17 years across software engineering, solution architecture and technical leadership.

Most of my career has been enterprise SaaS and platform work: healthcare, CRM, ERP, EdTech and business automation. My core stack is Angular, React, TypeScript, Node.js and NestJS, with PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB and Redis, and AWS, Docker, Kubernetes and CI/CD for delivery. I am strongest at API-first design, integration architecture, security with OAuth2, JWT and RBAC, and at turning business workflows into dependable production systems.

As a lead, I run architecture reviews, technology selection, mentoring and technical planning, and I communicate with stakeholders in plain language.

On AI, I use Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Claude and ChatGPT in my daily work, and I work with LLM integrations, RAG, agentic workflows, context engineering and MCP, always with human review of the output.

My deepest strength is engineering and architecture, and I would be straightforward that Power Platform is where I am still building depth: <fill in: your actual Power Platform and Microsoft exposure, if any>. What I bring is the engineering discipline underneath it: ALM, environments, integration, security and team leadership, and I have a concrete plan to close the platform gap."

## Why this shape works

- **Present, past, future**, ending on the role.
- One sentence of honesty about the gap builds trust and pre-empts the obvious question.
- Labelled content: the experience and tool lists above are **Verified professional experience**; Power Platform depth is **Preparation required** unless you fill in more.

## Details to confirm before the interview

- Your current title and employer wording.
- <fill in: one proud outcome, with a verifiable fact>
- <fill in: Power Platform or Microsoft exposure you can truthfully state>

## Common mistake

Listing every technology and never mentioning the role. Also avoid claiming Power Platform or agent-framework expertise you cannot defend in the next question.
followUps: Which single project best proves you can lead this crew?
What is your honest level with Power Platform today?
How do you check the output of AI tools you use?

questions.title: Why WPP, and why the AI COE Engineering Lead role?
questions.quick: As I understand the role, it leads a crew of six to ten engineers inside a global Cloud Apps and AI programme, building on the Power Platform and an agent ecosystem, with ALM discipline, research spikes, Kanban flow and a clean handover to support. That combines what I do best, which is architecture, standards and team leadership, with the AI direction I want to deepen. WPP's scale makes reusable, governed patterns matter. I would add engineering rigour and I am clear about the Power Platform depth I will build.
questions.revision: Tie the role's real elements to your verified strengths: lead a crew, ALM and standards, AI spikes, Kanban delivery, support handover; be honest about the platform gap.
questions.detailed:
Answer from the **job description**, not from generic praise of the brand.

## What the role asks for (as I read the JD)

- A global **Cloud Apps and AI programme**.
- A **crew of 6 to 10 engineers** to lead.
- A **Power Platform plus agent ecosystem** as the delivery surface.
- **ALM** (application lifecycle management) across environments.
- **Research spikes** to test new AI and platform options.
- **Kanban** delivery and a proper **handover to support**.

## How my background maps

| JD element | Honest mapping |
|---|---|
| Lead a crew | Verified professional experience: mentoring, architecture reviews, technical planning |
| ALM and handover | Verified: CI/CD, production deployment, engineering standards across applications |
| Research spikes | Conceptual and applied: LLM integration, RAG, agentic workflows, MCP |
| Power Platform | Preparation required |

## Spoken answer

"Three things attract me. First, the programme is global, so patterns have to be reusable and governed, which is where architecture and standards pay off. Second, an AI COE needs someone who can turn experiments into supported products: spikes, then ALM, then handover to support. That is the discipline I bring from production delivery. Third, I want to lead a crew of this size where I can still read the design and review the code. On the Power Platform side, I am building depth deliberately and I will tell you exactly where I am today: <fill in: current Power Platform status>."

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: what you know about WPP's AI and Cloud Apps work from public sources, stated only if you have read it>
- <fill in: one reason this programme specifically attracts you>
- Check the latest JD wording, since it may differ from this summary.

## Common mistake

Praising the company's size or awards without linking to the work. Also avoid implying you already know their internal platform.
followUps: What would you want to learn about our programme in your first month?
How does an AI COE differ from a normal delivery team?
What attracts you about a lead role rather than an individual architect role?

questions.title: Tell me about the CallHealth RealTimeControlTower project in 30 seconds
questions.quick: RealTimeControlTower, or RTCT, was a real-time analytics initiative for the CallHealth platform. It helped decision-makers and CXOs monitor operational performance by bringing together data from multiple business sources into operational dashboards and KPI reports. My focus was data freshness, consistency, reliability and performance, plus monitoring and troubleshooting so leaders could trust the numbers. My specific role was <fill in: your role on RTCT>, and the outcome was <fill in: verified outcome, no invented metrics>.
questions.revision: RTCT: real-time operational analytics for CallHealth leaders; many sources, dashboards, KPIs, trusted data. State your role and one verified outcome.
questions.detailed:
This is the **30-second executive summary**: context, purpose, your angle, one outcome.

## Spoken version

"RealTimeControlTower was a real-time analytics initiative for the CallHealth platform. The goal was to let decision-makers and CXOs monitor operational performance without waiting for manual reports. It integrated several business data sources into operational dashboards and KPI reporting. The engineering challenge was keeping the data fresh, consistent and reliable while the system stayed fast and supportable. I was <fill in: role and scope>, and the result was <fill in: verified outcome>."

## What is verified, and what is not

**Verified professional experience (themes only):** real-time data aggregation and analytics; integrating multiple business data sources; operational dashboards and KPI reporting; data freshness, consistency and reliability; performance; monitoring and troubleshooting; executive reporting.

**Not confirmed, so left as placeholders:** the number of data sources, refresh interval, user counts, technologies used inside RTCT, team size, dates and measured results.

## Why this wording works

It leads with the business purpose, uses the audience (CXOs) to explain why freshness and trust matter, and ends with a prompt for follow-up questions, which lets the interviewer choose the depth. Compare with the two-minute and ten-minute versions in this set.

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: your exact role and responsibilities>
- <fill in: number and types of data sources>
- <fill in: one verified outcome, qualitative if no figures are approved>

## Common mistake

Quoting numbers such as latency or user counts from memory. If a figure is not verified, say what you owned and what you observed, not a statistic.
followUps: What data sources did it combine?
What did you personally build or decide?
How did you define real time for that audience?

questions.title: Walk me through the CallHealth RealTimeControlTower project in two minutes
questions.quick: RTCT gave CallHealth leaders a live view of operational performance. The problem was fragmented, slow reporting. I helped design how multiple business data sources were aggregated, kept fresh and made consistent, then shown as operational dashboards and KPIs for decision-makers and CXOs. I cared about reliability, performance and clear monitoring so support could trace any wrong number. My contribution was <fill in: specifics>. The lesson I carry forward is to define each metric once and show freshness openly.
questions.revision: Problem, users, approach, my contribution, challenge, lesson. Themes verified; specifics are placeholders to fill in.
questions.detailed:
A two-minute answer follows **context, approach, contribution, challenge, result, lesson**.

## Spoken version (about 2 minutes)

**Context.** "CallHealth is a healthcare platform. Leaders needed to see operational performance as it happened rather than in delayed reports. RealTimeControlTower, or RTCT, was the real-time analytics initiative for that."

**Users.** "The audience was decision-makers and CXOs, so the output had to be trustworthy and quick to read."

**Approach.** "We aggregated data from multiple business sources, kept it fresh and consistent, and presented it through operational dashboards and KPI reporting. I focused on <fill in: your focus, for example data flow, API layer, dashboard performance>."

**Challenge.** "The hard parts in this kind of system are consistency across sources, freshness versus load, and being able to explain a number when someone questions it. We handled that with <fill in: verified mechanism>."

**Result.** "<fill in: verified outcome>."

**Lesson.** "Define every metric once, show a last-updated time, and build monitoring from day one, because executives lose trust faster than they gain it."

## Labelling

- **Verified professional experience:** the themes above.
- **Preparation required:** all concrete numbers and technologies.

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: number of data sources and their types>
- <fill in: refresh approach and target freshness>
- <fill in: your exact contribution>

questions.title: Give a ten-minute technical deep dive on the CallHealth RealTimeControlTower
questions.quick: I structure a deep dive in twenty points: business problem, users, requirements, architecture, components, data contracts, authentication and authorisation, decisions and rejected alternatives, scalability, reliability, security, testing and delivery, observability, my contribution, challenges, lessons, improvements today and relevance to the AI COE. For RTCT the verified themes are real-time aggregation, multiple sources, dashboards, freshness, consistency and monitoring. Every unconfirmed specific stays a placeholder until I have checked it.
questions.revision: Use the 20-point narrative: problem to lessons to AI COE relevance. Themes are verified; every specific is a placeholder to confirm.
questions.detailed:
A ten-minute deep dive needs a **fixed narrative** so you never lose the thread. Use the points below, roughly 30 seconds each. Everything marked with angle brackets is a placeholder: do not state it until confirmed.

{{diagram:rtct-asis}}

9. **Decisions and rejected alternatives:** <fill in: at least one decision, one rejected option, and why>.

Number of sources, refresh intervals, data volumes, technologies, team size, dates, outcomes. If any is not verifiable, say "I would need to check the exact figure".

## Common mistake

questions.title: How would you redesign RTCT today with modern architecture and AI?
questions.quick: This is a proposed future design, not history. I would ingest from each source through contract-checked connectors, publish events, process them asynchronously with idempotent handlers, and store both raw events and read-optimised aggregates. Dashboards would read from aggregates, with freshness SLOs shown on screen. I would add structured logging, metrics and alerting, least-privilege access, and optionally a governed natural-language analytics layer over approved metrics only.
questions.revision: PROPOSED design: contract-first ingestion, events, idempotent processing, raw plus aggregate storage, freshness SLOs, observability, least privilege, optional governed NL analytics.
questions.detailed:
**Important: this is a PROPOSED future design, not a description of what RTCT used.** Say so at the start of your answer.

{{diagram:rtct-proposed}}

## Design

1. **Ingestion.** One connector per source, each validated against a **versioned data contract** (schema, units, identifiers, timestamps). Bad records go to a quarantine queue, not silently dropped.
2. **Event-driven processing.** Connectors publish events; consumers aggregate asynchronously. Handlers are **idempotent** so retries and replays are safe, and late data is handled by event time.
3. **Storage.** Keep immutable raw events for replay and audit, plus **read-optimised aggregates** for dashboards. <fill in: store choice, for example PostgreSQL or a columnar store, after evaluating volumes>
4. **Semantic layer.** Each KPI defined once, with owner and formula, so every dashboard agrees.
5. **Dashboards.** Read only from aggregates; show **last updated** and a freshness status.
6. **Freshness SLOs.** For example, "95 percent of KPI updates visible within <fill in: agreed target>". SLOs are agreed with stakeholders, not invented by engineering.
7. **Observability.** Structured logs with correlation IDs, metrics for lag, error and quarantine rates, alerts on SLO burn, and runbooks for support.
8. **Security.** OAuth2 or OIDC login, RBAC down to KPI and tenant level, secrets in a vault, encrypted transport, audit of access.
9. **Optional natural-language analytics.** An LLM translates a question into a query over the **approved semantic layer only**, never raw tables, with permission checks, query logging and a visible "how this was calculated" explanation. Treat as an experiment behind a research spike first.

## Trade-offs

Events add operational complexity compared with scheduled batch jobs. For low volume, a simpler polling and aggregation job may be better. The right choice depends on the freshness target and volume.

## Details to confirm before the interview

Which cloud services the real project used, if you compare; do not claim any. Which of these ideas you have built elsewhere.

## Common mistake

Presenting the redesign as if it was delivered, or over-engineering with streaming when the required freshness is a few minutes.

diagrams.title: Proposed RTCT redesign
diagrams.alt: A proposed, not historical, design: sources pass through contract-checked connectors into an event stream, idempotent processors write raw events and aggregates, a semantic layer feeds dashboards and an optional governed natural-language layer, with observability and security across it.

followUps: When would you keep batch instead of events?
How would you stop a natural-language layer from leaking data?
How do you test freshness SLOs?

questions.title: Walk me through your enterprise SaaS, CRM, ERP and EdTech platform experience
questions.quick: Thirty-second version: I have built and architected enterprise SaaS, CRM, ERP and EdTech platforms, with multi-tenancy, API-first design, business workflows, integrations, dashboards and access control. I focused on modular architecture and reusable shared services, and on production operations and CI/CD. Two-minute version adds how I decide module boundaries, how tenants and roles are isolated, how integrations are contracted, and my own role: <fill in: scope, team size, and verified outcomes>.
questions.revision: Themes: multi-tenancy, API-first, workflows, integrations, dashboards, access control, modular architecture, shared services, CI/CD. Add real specifics.
questions.detailed:
Give both versions in one flow: the short one first, then expand if the interviewer leans in.

## 30-second version

"Across my career I have built enterprise SaaS, CRM, ERP and EdTech platforms. The common themes are multi-tenancy, API-first design, business workflows, integrations, dashboards and role-based access, delivered as modular systems with reusable shared services and disciplined CI/CD."

## Two-minute version

1. **Domains.** SaaS, CRM, ERP and EdTech. <fill in: which products, and your role on each>
2. **Architecture.** Modular structure with clear boundaries; I choose between a modular monolith and microservices according to team size and change rate. <fill in: which you used where>
3. **Multi-tenancy.** Tenant identity carried through every request and enforced on the server. <fill in: isolation model>
4. **API-first.** Contracts agreed before implementation so front end, integrations and partners work in parallel.
5. **Workflows and integrations.** Business processes modelled as explicit states, with integrations that tolerate failure. <fill in: example integration>
6. **Access control.** RBAC with JWT or OAuth2-based authentication.
7. **Operations.** CI/CD, production deployment and troubleshooting. <fill in: environments and tooling>
8. **Shared services.** Reusable components for authentication, notifications and similar cross-cutting needs. <fill in: examples>

## Labelling

Themes are **Verified professional experience**. Product names, scale, team sizes and results are **Preparation required**.

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: product names you may disclose>
- <fill in: number of applications and teams>
- <fill in: a verified result for each domain>

## Common mistake

Describing four domains at the same shallow level. Choose the one closest to the AI COE, for example integration-heavy workflows, and go deeper there.
followUps: Which platform are you most proud of and why?
How did you isolate tenant data?
How did shared services avoid becoming a bottleneck?

questions.title: How have you set engineering standards across multiple applications?
questions.quick: I set standards by making the right way the easy way. That means shared templates and reusable components, agreed API conventions, a common CI/CD pipeline with quality gates, code review checklists and short architecture decision records. I keep the standard small, explain the reason behind each rule, and review adoption through architecture reviews and mentoring rather than policing. The concrete standards I introduced were <fill in: examples>, and the effect was <fill in: verified effect>.
questions.revision: Small, explained standards delivered as templates, pipelines, reviews and decision records; measure adoption; allow justified exceptions.
questions.detailed:
Standards across several applications fail when they are documents nobody uses. My approach is to **embed them in tooling**.

## Themes (Verified professional experience)

- **Reusable components and shared services** so teams do not rebuild authentication, logging or notifications.
- **CI/CD and engineering standards across applications**: shared pipeline stages for build, test, security scan and deploy.
- **API conventions**: naming, error format, versioning, pagination.
- **Review practice**: architecture reviews for significant changes and a lightweight code review checklist.
- **Decision records** for choices that others will later question.

## How I introduce them

1. Find the pain first (inconsistent errors, slow releases, repeated bugs).
2. Draft the smallest useful rule with the reason beside it.
3. Provide a starter template or shared library so compliance costs nothing.
4. Pilot on one application, then roll out.
5. Review adoption in architecture reviews and pair sessions.
6. Allow documented exceptions; a standard without an exception route is ignored.

## Relevance to an AI COE

The same ideas apply to AI work: prompt and evaluation conventions, review of AI-generated code, environment promotion for Power Platform solutions, and a definition of done that includes support handover.

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: three standards you actually introduced>
- <fill in: number of applications or teams covered>
- <fill in: a verified before and after, qualitative if no figures>

## Common mistake

Saying you "enforced" standards. Describe how you earned adoption and how you handled disagreement.
followUps: How did you handle a team that resisted a standard?
How do you keep standards from slowing delivery?
What would an AI-specific standard look like?

questions.title: Describe your experience with AI-assisted development and agentic AI
questions.quick: In three honest tiers. Verified practice: I use Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Claude and ChatGPT for coding, review, documentation and analysis. Working knowledge: LLM integrations, RAG, agentic workflows, context engineering and MCP. What I have taken to prototype or production is <fill in: specifics>. I treat AI output as a draft: I review it, run tests, check security and keep ownership of the design.
questions.revision: Three tiers: verified tool use, working concepts, and a clearly stated prototype versus production split; AI output is a draft to be verified.
questions.detailed:
Interviewers want honesty about depth. Use **three tiers** and label each.

## Tier 1: Verified professional experience

Day-to-day use of **Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Claude and ChatGPT** for code generation, refactoring, test drafts, documentation and requirements analysis.

## Tier 2: Conceptual knowledge

**LLM integrations, RAG, agentic workflows, context engineering and MCP.** I can explain: retrieval with permission filters, tool calling with least-privilege tools, why context quality drives output quality, and where agents need human approval gates.

## Tier 3: Implemented or prototype

<fill in: what you actually built, labelled as implemented in production, prototype, or conceptual only>. State it exactly. If it was only a prototype, say so.

## How I verify AI output

1. Read every generated change as I would a colleague's pull request.
2. Run tests and add missing ones; AI-written tests can pass for the wrong reason.
3. Check security: injection, secrets, permissions, dependency choices.
4. Keep prompts and context specific, and never paste confidential data into unapproved tools.
5. Record decisions that AI suggested and I accepted, so the reasoning is traceable.

## Frameworks and tools I have not used

I have not yet used Microsoft Agent Framework, Semantic Kernel, AutoGen, Claude Code, Windsurf or similar tools in production, and I will not claim them. The transferable parts are tool-calling design, orchestration, evaluation and guardrails, and my plan is a short spike to build a working agent with approval gates.

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: AI features or prototypes you built, with status>
- <fill in: any team practices for AI review you introduced>

## Common mistake

Claiming agentic expertise from reading and demos. Offer one concrete example, however small, with its limits.
followUps: Describe a case where AI output was wrong and how you caught it.
How would you design guardrails for an agent that can call business systems?
What would an evaluation approach for an agent look like?

questions.title: What is your experience with the Microsoft Power Platform and Dataverse?
questions.quick: I have some professional context with Power Apps, Power Automate, SharePoint, Microsoft 365, Dataverse and SQL Server, alongside JavaScript, TypeScript, REST and application permissions. My depth is <fill in: years, scenarios and level>, and I would not overstate it. What transfers strongly is data modelling, integration, security and ALM thinking, and I have a 30-day plan to build practical Power Platform depth.
questions.revision: Honest: some professional context, depth is a placeholder; map transferable concepts; show a concrete 30-day learning plan.
questions.detailed:
Be accurate about depth. The verified fact is **some professional context**; years, depth, plug-in work and certifications are **not confirmed**.

## Honest answer shape

"I have some professional context with Power Apps, Power Automate, SharePoint, Microsoft 365, Dataverse and SQL Server, together with JavaScript, TypeScript, REST and application permissions. My level is <fill in: specifics>. I have not yet built Dataverse plug-ins in production. Here is how my existing skills map across, and here is what I am doing about the rest."

## Transferable concepts

| Power Platform area | Transferable strength |
|---|---|
| Dataverse tables and relationships | Relational modelling in PostgreSQL and MySQL |
| Security roles | RBAC and application security |
| Power Automate flows | Event-driven and asynchronous processing |
| Custom connectors and Web API | REST and integration architecture |
| Solutions and environments | CI/CD, deployment and ALM |
| Power Apps component code | JavaScript and TypeScript |

## 30-day learning plan

- **Week 1:** Solutions, environments, managed and unmanaged solutions, and a Power Platform pipeline walk-through.
- **Week 2:** Dataverse tables, relationships, security roles and the Web API; build a small model.
- **Week 3:** Power Automate expressions, error handling, child flows and connection references.
- **Week 4:** Solution deployment with PAC CLI, a plug-in concept spike, and a short write-up of what I learned.

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: years and scenarios of Power Platform use>
- <fill in: whether you have built canvas apps, model-driven apps or flows>
- <fill in: certifications held, if any>

## Common mistake

Name-dropping Dataverse features you cannot discuss. One accurate example beats five claims.
followUps: Explain how a Dataverse security role differs from application RBAC you built.
How would you structure a solution for dev, test and production?
What is a plug-in and when would you avoid one?

questions.title: Your background is Node.js, Angular and React: how does it translate to this Power Platform-centred role?

My Node.js, Angular and React background maps to custom connectors, component code, APIs and integration. The real gaps are platform specifics such as Dataverse plug-ins, PAC CLI and solution ALM, and I would close them with a plan. I also bring team leadership and AI-assisted engineering.

Answer with a **fit matrix** and keep the three labels visible.

{{diagram:fit-flow}}

| Lead a crew of 6 to 10 engineers | Verified professional experience | Mentoring, architecture reviews, planning; <fill in: team sizes led> |

## Spoken answer

"The honest summary is that about two thirds of the role maps directly to what I do, and the rest is platform-specific. I am not hiding it: I would ramp quickly on Power Platform ALM and Dataverse, using my CI/CD and data-modelling background. If the crew includes Power Platform specialists, my job is to lead, set the engineering bar and connect the platform to wider architecture."

(Avoid the "two thirds" figure unless you have actually assessed it; replace with <fill in: your own assessment>.)

## Details to confirm before the interview

Current JD wording, who the Power Platform specialists on the crew are, and your actual exposure.

## Common mistake

Saying "it is all just APIs". Low-code platforms have their own limits, licensing and governance, and interviewers will test that.

diagrams.alt: Verified strengths in Node.js, Angular, React, APIs, security and leadership map to transferable skills like integration, data modelling and CI/CD, which together with a learning plan on Power Platform ALM and Dataverse lead to readiness for the AI COE role.

- **Solution architecture (PL-600 area):** 17+ years of solution architecture, architecture reviews, technology selection and stakeholder communication. Power Platform-specific architecture is **Preparation required**.
- **AI solutions (AI-102 area):** LLM integrations, RAG and agentic concepts; <fill in: implemented work>.
- **Cloud development (AZ-204 area):** AWS, Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD, REST and security patterns that transfer to Azure services. Azure-specific hands-on is **Preparation required**: <fill in: your Azure exposure>.

## About PL-600

Microsoft Learn shows the **PL-600 exam retiring on 30 June 2026**. Since the date has passed, re-check the current Microsoft Learn pages for PL-600, AI-102 and AZ-204, including any replacement certifications, before the interview and quote only what you confirmed. Existing exam pages and role-based credentials may have changed.

## Plan template

- <fill in: target certification and exam date>
- Weekly study hours, practice labs, and which concept maps to your daily work.
- Offer to share progress with the hiring manager.

## Details to confirm before the interview

Your status for each exam, whether the JD says "required" or "preferred", and the current Microsoft Learn status.

## Common mistake

Saying "equivalent experience" without an example. Always pair it with a concrete project or a dated plan.
followUps: Would you accept a conditional start with a certification deadline?
How do you prove architectural competence without a certificate?
Which exam would you take first, and why?

questions.title: How would you lead a crew of 6 to 10 engineers here? Describe your first 90 days
questions.quick: In the first 30 days I listen, map the work, the people and the environments, and fix one visible friction. By 60 days I introduce light standards: ALM, definition of done, Kanban limits and review practice, and start a first research spike. By 90 days I run a stable cadence, show measurable flow metrics, and have a clean handover process to support. I adapt to what the crew already does well.
questions.revision: 30 days listen and map; 60 days standards, ALM, Kanban and a spike; 90 days stable flow, metrics and a support handover.
questions.detailed:
A good leadership answer is **specific, humble and measurable**.

{{diagram:plan-90}}

## Days 1 to 30: listen and map

- One-to-ones with every engineer: strengths, frustrations, aspirations.
- Map the programme: stakeholders, backlog, environments, deployment path, support model.
- Read the main solutions and agents with the crew.
- Fix **one visible friction** quickly to earn trust.

## Days 31 to 60: set the bar

- Agree a **definition of done** including tests, documentation and support handover.
- Establish **ALM**: environments, solution promotion, naming, source control.
- Shape **Kanban**: visible columns, work-in-progress limits, a blocked lane.
- Start the first **research spike** with a clear question, a time box and a decision at the end.
- Set up pairing and review practice, and help specialists share knowledge.

## Days 61 to 90: stabilise and show results

- Track simple flow metrics: cycle time, work in progress, blocked time. Agree targets with the team first.
- Run a handover to support for at least one item, using a checklist.
- Retrospective on what to keep, change and stop.
- Share a roadmap of spikes and a skills plan for the crew.

## Leadership principles

Clarity of priorities, psychological safety, delegating ownership, and being technical enough to review designs. For Power Platform, I would rely on specialists in the crew while I learn alongside them.

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: team sizes you have led and your own examples of each step>
- <fill in: Kanban or agile practice you have used>

## Common mistake

Arriving with a finished process. Propose a plan and invite the crew to shape it.

diagrams.title: First 90 days plan
diagrams.alt: A 90-day leadership plan: days 1 to 30 listen and map, days 31 to 60 set standards, ALM, Kanban and a first spike, days 61 to 90 stabilise flow, measure it and hand over to support.

followUps: What would you do if two senior engineers disagree strongly?
How would you handle an underperformer?
How do you balance spikes with delivery?

questions.title: Tell me about a time you resolved a difficult technical blocker
questions.quick: I use the STAR structure: situation, task, action and result. I choose a story where I owned the diagnosis, show how I narrowed the problem with evidence, explain the decision and trade-off, and finish with a verified result and what I changed to prevent recurrence. The real story I will tell is <fill in: your project, problem and outcome>. If I need an illustration, I label it as hypothetical so nothing is mistaken for fact.
questions.revision: STAR: situation, task, action, result; pick a story with your own diagnosis, evidence and prevention; label any hypothetical clearly.
questions.detailed:
Use **your own real story** in the interview. The template and example below help you prepare.

## Choosing the story

- You personally owned the diagnosis or decision.
- It involved evidence, not luck.
- It has a verifiable result and a lesson.
- It relates to the role: integration, performance, data consistency or deployment.

## STAR template

- **Situation:** <fill in: system, date range, impact>
- **Task:** <fill in: what you were responsible for>
- **Action:** hypothesis, evidence gathered (logs, metrics, reproduction), options considered, the decision and who you involved. <fill in: steps>
- **Result:** <fill in: verified outcome>; the prevention you added (monitoring, test, runbook).
- **Reflection:** what you would do earlier next time.

## Hypothetical example (clearly hypothetical, not my history)

*Situation:* a dashboard refresh intermittently showed stale KPIs. *Task:* find the cause without disrupting users. *Action:* compared source timestamps with processed timestamps, found a retry path that reprocessed a batch out of order, added idempotency keys and a lag alert, and confirmed with a replay test. *Result:* stale readings stopped and support gained a freshness alert. This example illustrates the shape only; do not present it as your story.

## Details to confirm before the interview

Which real story you will use, what you may disclose, and the figures you can verify.

## Common mistake

Spending most of the time on the situation. Aim for roughly 20 percent context and 60 percent action.
followUps: What would you do differently now?
Who else was involved and what did you ask of them?
How did you stop it happening again?

questions.title: Tell me about a time you disagreed with an architecture decision or a stakeholder
questions.quick: I use STAR and focus on how I disagreed. I state the other view fairly, bring evidence such as a small prototype or a comparison of options and costs, propose a way to decide, and commit to the outcome even if it is not mine. My real example is <fill in: your story and result>. I can also describe a clearly hypothetical case to show the pattern.
questions.revision: Disagree with evidence and respect: restate their view, compare options, propose a decision method, then commit; label any hypothetical.
questions.detailed:
The interviewer is testing **judgement and collaboration**, not who was right.

## STAR template

- **Situation:** <fill in: decision, stakeholders and stakes>
- **Task:** your responsibility for the outcome.
- **Action:** restated the other side fairly; gathered evidence (benchmark, prototype, cost, risk); proposed a decision method such as a time-boxed spike or an architecture decision record; escalated respectfully if needed.
- **Result:** <fill in: verified outcome>. Include when you were wrong or the decision went the other way.
- **Reflection:** what you learned about influencing.

## Hypothetical example (clearly hypothetical, not my history)

*Situation:* a stakeholder wanted a custom service for a workflow that a platform's built-in automation could cover. *Task:* recommend the right approach. *Action:* I acknowledged the delivery-speed argument, listed requirements the platform might not meet (volume, error handling, testing), ran a one-week spike on both, and wrote a decision record. *Result:* the team chose the built-in option with a defined extension point, and I supported it. This illustrates the pattern only.

## Choosing your real story

Pick one where the relationship stayed intact, you used evidence, and you accepted the decision. Avoid stories that blame a colleague.

## Details to confirm before the interview

The real example, what can be disclosed, and the actual outcome.

## Common mistake

Telling a story where you were simply right. Show that you tested your own assumptions.
followUps: What if the stakeholder still disagreed after the evidence?
Tell me about a time you were wrong.
How do you record decisions so they are not reopened?

questions.title: What are your gaps for this role, and how will you close them?
questions.quick: My gaps are platform-specific rather than engineering fundamentals: Power Platform ALM and PAC CLI, Dataverse Web API and plug-ins, an agent framework spike, Power Automate expressions and Kanban metrics. My four-week plan takes them in that order, each ending with a small working artefact I can show. I also have not confirmed certifications, so my plan includes the current Microsoft Learn status.
questions.revision: Name the gaps plainly and give a four-week plan with an artefact each week: ALM and PAC CLI, Dataverse, agent spike, Power Automate and Kanban.
questions.detailed:
Naming gaps with a plan is a strength. Group them as **Preparation required**.

## Gap list

1. Power Platform ALM and PAC CLI.
2. Dataverse Web API and plug-ins.
3. Agent framework, such as Microsoft Agent Framework (spike only).
4. Power Automate expressions and robust error handling.
5. Kanban metrics for a team of this size.
6. Certification status: <fill in: current status>.

## Four-week priority study plan

| Week | Focus | Artefact to show |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Solutions, environments, PAC CLI authentication, import and export, a simple pipeline | A scripted solution deployment between two environments |
| 2 | Dataverse tables, security roles, Web API calls, plug-in concepts | A small Dataverse model with Web API queries |
| 3 | Agent framework spike: tool calling, approval gate, evaluation | A small agent with one tool and logged decisions |
| 4 | Power Automate expressions, error handling, and Kanban flow metrics | A resilient flow plus a cycle-time dashboard template |

## What already helps

CI/CD, REST integration, relational modelling, RBAC and OAuth2, LLM and RAG concepts, and leadership are **Verified professional experience** or transferable.

## How to say it

"I have not yet used these in production, so I will not claim them. I have scoped four weeks, and I will share what I produce."

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: any of these gaps you have already started on, with dates>
- <fill in: how many hours per week you can commit>

## Common mistake

Calling a strength a weakness, or listing gaps without a plan or evidence of progress.
followUps: Which gap worries you most and why?
How will you learn while leading a team?
What would you have ready by your first day?

questions.title: What questions should you ask the interviewer?
questions.quick: I ask about the crew and its skill mix, how success is measured in the first year, how research spikes become supported products, the ALM and environment model, how agents are governed, how Kanban and handover to support work today, the biggest technical risk, and how the team learns. These show I think about delivery, governance and people, not only technology.
questions.revision: Ask about crew, success measures, spike-to-product path, ALM, governance, flow, support handover, risks and learning.
questions.detailed:
Choose four or five, ordered by what the conversation has not already covered.

## Ten strong questions

**Team and leadership**

1. What is the current skill mix in the crew, and where do you most need the lead to add strength?
2. What does success look like for this role at six and twelve months?

**Delivery**

3. How does Kanban work today: work-in-progress limits, metrics and who sets priorities?
4. What does a good handover to support look like, and what has gone wrong in the past?
5. How are research spikes chosen, time-boxed and turned into decisions?

**Platform and architecture**

6. What is the ALM model across environments for Power Platform solutions, and what pipeline tooling is used?
7. How are agents and AI features governed: approvals, evaluation, data access and audit?
8. Which parts of the Cloud Apps and AI programme are most reusable across regions?

**Risk and growth**

9. What is the biggest technical or organisational risk you see for the programme?
10. How does the team keep learning, and is there support for certifications and conference time?

## Why these work

They show lead-level thinking: ALM, governance, flow and people. Avoid questions answered on the careers page, and avoid salary in a technical round unless invited.

## Details to confirm before the interview

Adjust the wording to what the JD actually says, and drop any question already answered. <fill in: one question specific to the interviewer's background>

## Common mistake

Asking nothing, or asking only about benefits. Take notes and reference answers in your closing.
followUps: Which question would you ask first and why?
What would a worrying answer sound like?
How do you follow up after the interview?

questions.title: What is a strong elevator closing statement for this interview?
questions.quick: I would close by saying that I bring 17 years of enterprise architecture and fullstack leadership, a delivery mindset built on ALM, standards and production support, and a practical, verified approach to AI-assisted engineering. I am clear about my Power Platform gap and I have a plan to close it quickly. I would be glad to lead the crew and turn research spikes into supported products.
questions.revision: Close with experience, delivery discipline, AI practice, honest gap with a plan, and enthusiasm to lead the crew.
questions.detailed:
Keep the close to **30 seconds** and make it a summary of what the interviewer has heard, not new claims.

## Spoken version

"Thank you for the conversation. To summarise: I bring more than 17 years of enterprise architecture and fullstack engineering leadership, a delivery discipline built on ALM, engineering standards and clean handovers, and a practical, human-reviewed approach to AI-assisted development. I have been straightforward about where I am still building Power Platform depth, and I have a concrete four-week plan. I would like to lead this crew and help turn research spikes into supported products. <fill in: one specific thing you learned in this interview that excites you>."

## Elements

1. **Credibility:** experience and domains (Verified professional experience).
2. **Fit:** delivery discipline mapped to the JD.
3. **Honesty:** the gap and the plan (Preparation required).
4. **Enthusiasm:** a specific reason, tied to something said in the interview.
5. **Next step:** ask about timeline.

## Details to confirm before the interview

- <fill in: the detail from the interview you will reference>
- Your preferred availability and notice period, if asked.

## Common mistake

Repeating the full introduction or overselling. Also avoid apologising for gaps: state them calmly.

## Variations

If the interview ran long, shorten to two sentences: experience and fit, then the gap and plan. If it went very well, add one concrete idea you would explore in the first month, such as auditing how spikes become supported products. Always end by thanking the panel and asking about next steps.
followUps: What is the timeline for the next steps?
Is there anything about my background you would like me to clarify?
What would you want me to prepare before a next round?
